title: Camera 101: How to choose your game’s perspective
summary: A beginner’s guide to video game camera perspectives: top-down, side-scrolling, first-person, third-person, isometric, and fixed views, and the games each suits.
body_markdown:
## How to choose a perspective for your video game


There’s no single right answer, but a few questions can point you in the right direction.


### What does the player need to see?


A good camera shows players the information they need, follows what they control, and moves in ways that feel predictable and comfortable. Start by listing what players must see to play well. Do they need to see far ahead? All of the map at once? Their character’s every move? The answers will rule some views in and others out.


### Do you want closeness or control?


Views that sit far above the action, like top-down and isometric, give players a wide overview and a sense of being in charge. Views that sit close to the character, like third-person and first-person, put players in the middle of the action. Think about which feeling fits your game.


### How much world do you want to build?


2D views like side-scrolling and top-down only show the world from one direction, so you don’t need to build every side of every area. For a first game, that can save a lot of time.


### Will it be comfortable to play?


When the screen moves but your body doesn’t, the mismatch can make some people feel sick. It can happen in 2D games, but it’s worse in 3D and especially in VR. Smooth, predictable camera movement helps, and so do[comfort options](https://unity.com/blog/video-game-accessibility-basics) like an adjustable[field of view](https://unity.com/glossary/field-of-view) .


### Try your game idea in different views


A useful exercise is to picture the same idea through different cameras. Imagine a game about delivering mail around a small town. From top-down, it becomes a game about planning routes through streets. As a side-scroller, it’s about hopping fences and dodging dogs. In third-person, it’s about exploring the town and meeting its characters. In an isometric view, it could become a puzzle about moving objects to clear paths. Same idea, very different games – which is exactly why the camera matters.
